propositions.text: The Applicants are a Nigerian family of six with two US-born children who are applicants and two Canadian-born children who are not applicants.
propositions.quote: The Applicants are members of a family of six. The adult Applicants, Eddie Aigbe Idiagbonya [Principal Applicant] and his spouse, Becky Lee Ibharia [Spouse], are citizens of Nigeria. They have two children who were born in the United States [US] in 2016 and who hold US Citizenship. Those minor children are also applicants in this matter [Minor Applicants, collectively the Applicants]. Two other children were born in Canada after the family left the US in 2017 and entered Canada. The Canadian minor children are not applicants in this matter.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicants are a Nigerian family with two US-born applicant children and two Canadian-born non-applicant children.

propositions.text: The RPD denied the Applicants' refugee claim in January 2019, finding no established persecution risk or harm under IRPA sections 96 or 97.
propositions.quote: The Applicants’ claim for refugee protection was denied by the Refugee Protection Division [RPD] in January 2019. The Applicants asserted that they had a well-founded fear of persecution by the Principal Applicant’s family and, in particular, they feared female genital mutilation [FGM] of the Spouse who had refused to submit to same. The RPD rejected the claim. It found that the Applicants had not established that the Minor Applicants would be persecuted in the US or that they had reason to fear harm that would bring them under either s. 96 or s. 97 of Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [IRPA].

propositions.text: The RPD found a viable internal flight alternative (IFA) in Port Harcourt for the Applicants.
propositions.quote: Further, the RPD found that the Applicants had a viable internal flight alternative [IFA] in Port Harcourt.

propositions.text: The RAD upheld the RPD’s determination in October 2019.
propositions.quote: In October 2019, the Refugee Appeal Division [RAD] upheld the RPD’s determination.

propositions.text: An application for leave and judicial review was denied by this Court in September 2020.
propositions.quote: An application for leave and judicial review was denied by this Court in September 2020.

propositions.text: The Applicants then sought a Pre-Removal Risk Assessment (PRRA).
propositions.quote: The Applicants then sought a Pre-Removal Risk Assessment [PRRA].

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker (RPD) denied refugee protection, finding no persecution risk and a viable IFA; RAD upheld this; judicial review was denied; Applicants sought PRRA.

propositions.text: The PRRA Officer denied the PRRA application on December 13, 2023, finding no substantially different facts from prior proceedings.
propositions.quote: In a decision dated December 13, 2023, a senior immigration officer [PRRA Officer] denied the PRRA application. The PRRA Officer found that, overall, the submissions provided by the Principal Applicant did not establish any facts that are substantially different from those that were presented to the RPD and RAD.

propositions.text: The PRRA Officer found the Principal Applicant's facts materially consistent with prior arguments and unable to overcome RPD and RAD findings, including the viable IFA in Port Harcourt.
propositions.quote: The Principal Applicant had reiterated facts which were materially consistent with those already argued before the RPD and RAD and which were not capable of overcoming the findings of the RPD and RAD. Namely, the existence of a viable IFA for the Applicants in Port Harcourt.

propositions.text: The PRRA Officer found the risk from crime, terrorism, and kidnappings is generalized in Nigeria and not particular to the Applicants.
propositions.quote: With respect to the Principal Applicant’s claim that he and his family could not find safety anywhere in Nigeria due to crime, terrorism and kidnappings that have continued to occur all across the country, the PRRA Officer found that this risk is faced generally by others in Nigeria and is not particular to the Principal Applicant and his family.

propositions.text: The PRRA Officer found insufficient objective evidence that the Applicants face a generalized risk beyond that faced by others in Nigeria.
propositions.quote: The Principal Applicant had not provided sufficient objective evidence to demonstrate that, on a balance of probabilities, he and his family face a generalized risk that is not faced by others in Nigeria.

paragraphs.summary: The PRRA Officer denied the PRRA, finding no new facts, risk generalized in Nigeria, and insufficient evidence of personal risk beyond others.

propositions.text: The Applicants assert the PRRA Officer breached procedural fairness by not providing an oral hearing and erred in assessing evidence.
propositions.quote: The Applicants assert that the PRRA Officer: breached their right to procedural fairness by not providing them with an oral hearing, and erred in assessing their supporting evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicants argue the PRRA Officer breached procedural fairness by denying an oral hearing and erred in evidence assessment.

propositions.text: The standard of review for procedural fairness issues is correctness, focusing on fairness of procedure in all circumstances.
propositions.quote: The standard of review for issues of procedural fairness is correctness (see Mission Institution v Khela, 2014 SCC 24 at para 79; Canadian Association of Refugee Lawyers v Canada (Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship), 2020 FCA 196 at para 35). Functionally, this requires the Court’s analysis to focus on whether the procedure followed was fair, having regard to all the circumstances (Canadian Pacific Railway Company v Canada (Attorney General), 2018 FCA 69 at para 54).

paragraphs.summary: The court states the procedural fairness standard of review is correctness, focusing on fairness of procedure in context.

propositions.text: The court holds the standard of review for PRRA Officer's failure to hold oral hearing is reasonableness, not correctness.
propositions.quote: With respect to the question of whether the granting of an oral hearing is one of procedural fairness, requiring correctness as the standard of review, or one of mixed fact and law, attracting the standard of reasonableness, I have previously held and remain of the view that the standard of reasonableness applies because, as found in Ikechi v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FC 361 at para 26, a PRRA officer decides whether to hold an oral hearing by considering a PRRA application against the requirements in s 113(b) of the IRPA and the factors in s 167 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations SOR/2002-227[IRP Regulations].

propositions.text: Applying s 113(b) of IRPA is a mixed fact and law question, attracting reasonableness standard.
propositions.quote: Thus, applying s 113(b) is essentially a question of mixed fact and law (see, for example, Hare v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 73 at para 11; Balogh v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2022 FC 447 at paras 13 – 14).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the reasonableness standard applies to PRRA Officer's oral hearing decision, as it involves mixed fact and law under s 113(b) IRPA.

propositions.text: The standard of review for PRRA Officer's merits decision is reasonableness, requiring justification, transparency, and intelligibility.
propositions.quote: The standard of review applicable to the merits of the PRRA Officer’s decision is reasonableness (Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 [Vavilov] at para 25). On judicial review, the Court asks whether the decision bears the hallmarks of reasonableness – justification, transparency and intelligibility – and whether it is justified in relation to the relevant factual and legal constraints that bear on the decision (Vavilov, at para 99).

paragraphs.summary: The court states the PRRA Officer's merits decision is reviewed for reasonableness, requiring justification, transparency, and intelligibility.

propositions.text: The sole issue is whether the PRRA Officer’s decision was reasonable.
propositions.quote: For the foregoing reasons, in my view the sole issue arising in this matter is whether the PRRA Officer’s decision was reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies the sole issue as the reasonableness of the PRRA Officer's decision.

propositions.text: The Applicants submit the PRRA Officer did not identify contradictions but effectively disbelieved the Principal Applicant's affidavit, making a veiled credibility finding.
propositions.quote: The Applicants submit that the PRRA Officer did not clearly mention any contradiction, inconsistency, vagueness or other reasons to cast doubt on the truthfulness of the Principal Applicant’s sworn affidavit but, instead, found that their evidence was not sufficient to establish a risk. They submit that, in reaching this conclusion, the PRRA Officer essentially disbelieved the Principal Applicant’s sworn statement relating to the ongoing risk of persecution and his family members being targeted by the Applicants’ persecutors. The Principal Applicant therefore submits that the PRRA Officer made a veiled credibility finding. Accordingly, that Officer’s decision not to provide an oral hearing is a breach of procedural fairness because the PA’s credibility was at issue.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicants argue the PRRA Officer made a veiled credibility finding and breached procedural fairness by denying an oral hearing.

propositions.text: The PRRA Officer found the risk from crime and terrorism is generalized and not particular to the Applicants, rejecting the Applicants' assertion of credibility issues.
propositions.quote: The PRRA Officer’s finding at issue addressed the Applicant’s submission that they could not find safety anywhere in Nigeria due to crime, terrorism and kidnapping that occur all across the country. In that regard, the PRRA Office found: It is noted that this specified risk is faced generally by others in Nigeria and is not particular to the principal applicant and his family. Namely, the threat of harm emanating from criminal gangs and terrorist groups could indiscriminately confront any individual. In this light, I find the principal applicant has not provided sufficient objective evidence to demonstrate that, on a balance of probabilities, he and his family do not face a generalized risk that is faced by others in Nigeria.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the PRRA Officer did not disbelieve the Applicants but found the risk generalized and not particular to them.

propositions.text: The PRRA Officer found documentary evidence on Nigeria's security situation generalized and not linked to the Applicants' personal circumstances.
propositions.quote: The PRRA Officer went on to discuss the documentary evidence provided by the Applicants in support of their submission, which included articles and reports on the current security situation amid civil unrest in Nigeria from various media and research outlets. Having considered all these documents in the context of assessing country conditions, the PRRA Officer found that they were generalized in nature and did not establish a link directly to the Principal Applicant’s personal circumstances. Further, that evidence of general conditions within a country is not in itself sufficient to show that the Principal Applicant and his family are personally at risk of harm.

paragraphs.summary: The PRRA Officer found the documentary evidence generalized and insufficient to show personal risk to the Applicants.

propositions.text: The PRRA Officer did not err or make a credibility finding but found insufficient evidence of personal risk beyond generalized risk.
propositions.quote: In my view, the PRRA Officer did not err. It is clear from the reasons that the PRRA Office did not disbelieve the Principal Applicant and did not make a veiled or any credibility finding. Rather, as the Officer explained, the Applicants had not provided sufficient evidence to demonstrate that they personally were at risk. That is, that they faced a generalized risk that is not faced by others in Nigeria.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no error or credibility finding by the PRRA Officer, only insufficient evidence of personal risk.

propositions.text: Section 113(b) IRPA allows a hearing if a serious credibility issue arises related to protection factors and evidence is central and justifies protection.
propositions.quote: In the context of a PRRA, s.113(b) of the IRPA provides that “a hearing may be held if the Minister, on the basis of prescribed factors, is of the opinion that a hearing is required”. The prescribed factors are contained in s.167 of the IRP Regulations: (a) whether there is evidence that raises a serious issue of the applicant’s credibility and is related to the factors set out in sections 96 and 97 of the Act; (b) whether the evidence is central to the decision with respect to the application for protection; and (c) whether the evidence, if accepted, would justify allowing the application for protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains s.113(b) IRPA allows a hearing if serious credibility issues arise and evidence is central and justifies protection.

propositions.text: No serious credibility issue was found, so no legal basis existed for an oral hearing in this case.
propositions.quote: Thus, a PRRA Officer may hold a hearing if they believe one is required where a serious issue of credibility arises. I agree with the Respondent that in this case, no such finding was made, and that without a serious issue of credibility, the PRRA Officer had no reason to convoke, or legal basis to justify, an oral hearing ( Jystina v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 912 at para 28).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no serious credibility issue existed, so no legal basis for an oral hearing was present.

propositions.text: The Applicants submit the PRRA Officer failed to reference evidence of attacks on family members and ongoing persecution threats.
propositions.quote: The Applicants submit that the PRRA Officer made no specific reference to any of their evidence submitted in support of the PRRA, including a claim that the Applicants’ persecutors recently attacked the Principal Applicant’s mother and her brother because of their desire to force the Principal Applicant’s spouse and daughters to undergo FGM. The Principal Applicant asserted in his affidavit submitted to the PRRA Officer that the Applicants cannot return to Nigeria because their persecutors constantly harass their family members in order to reach them and are very well-connected throughout Nigeria. Their connections with politicians and police would enable the persecutors to easily locate the Applicants.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicants argue the PRRA Officer failed to address evidence of attacks and ongoing persecution threats.

propositions.text: The Applicants claim the PRRA Officer unreasonably concluded new evidence was substantially the same as prior facts.
propositions.quote: The Applicants claim that PRRA Officer failed to assess this new evidence as to their persecutors’ ongoing interest in finding and harming them and unreasonably concluded that the new evidence contained substantially the same facts as previously presented.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicants claim the PRRA Officer unreasonably treated new evidence as substantially the same as prior facts.

propositions.text: The PRRA Officer stated they carefully considered all documentary evidence and that negative RPD decisions must be respected absent new evidence affecting outcome.
propositions.quote: I note that in their reasons the PRRA Officer states that they have read and carefully considered all of the documentary evidence material presented in and associated with an in support of the PRRA. Further, that a negative refugee determination by the RPD must be respected by a PRRA officer, unless there is new evidence of facts that might have affected the outcome of the RPD hearing if the evidence had been presented to the RPD.

paragraphs.summary: The PRRA Officer considered all evidence and respects negative RPD decisions unless new evidence might affect outcome.

propositions.text: The PRRA Officer acknowledged the Principal Applicant's affidavit describing ongoing threats and attacks on family members by persecutors.
propositions.quote: The PRRA Officer acknowledged that the Principal Applicant had submitted an affidavit stating the reasons why that he was forced to flee from Nigeria. The PRRA Officer also states that, in his affidavit, the Principal Applicant explained that his family members are still highly motivated to locate and harm him and his family. Further, that in July 2022, members of his extended family entered his mother’s home and inquired as to the whereabouts of the Principal Applicant and his family. The Officer also acknowledges submissions that, upon receiving no information, family members attacked and physically assaulted his mother and uncle who sustained injuries requiring hospitalization, and that the Applicants’ persecutors are very well-connected with Nigerian politicians and police and would be able to locate them easily.

paragraphs.summary: The PRRA Officer acknowledged the affidavit describing ongoing threats and attacks on family members by persecutors.

propositions.text: The PRRA Officer found the submissions did not establish facts substantially different from those before RPD and RAD and reiterated the viable IFA finding.
propositions.quote: The PRRA Officer found that, overall, the submissions provided by the Principal Applicant did not establish any facts that were “substantially different” from those that were presented to the RPD and RAD. Rather, he had reiterated facts which are “materially consistent with” those already argued before the RPD and RAD and were not capable of overcoming their findings. Namely, the existence of a viable IFA for the applicants in Port Harcourt.

paragraphs.summary: The PRRA Officer found no substantially different facts and reiterated the viable IFA finding from prior decisions.

propositions.text: A PRRA is not an appeal but assesses new risk developments; prior negative RPD decisions must be respected absent new evidence affecting outcome.
propositions.quote: I do not agree with the Applicants that it was an error for the PRRA Officer to require them to overcome prior findings of the RPD and the RAD. It is well established that a PRRA application is not an appeal or reconsideration of a negative decision of the RPD or RAD. Rather, it is intended to assess new risk developments between the hearing and the removal date (see, for example, Raza v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) at para 12 [Raza]; Ponniah v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FC 386 at para 27; Kaybaki v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2004 FC 32 at para 11; Nam v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2011 FC 1298 at para 22). In that regard, the evidence that may be admitted at a PRRA is limited by s. 113(a) of the IRPA. As held by the Federal Court of Appeal in Raza, s. 113(a) is “based on the premise that a negative refugee determination by the RPD must be respected by the PRRA officer, unless there is new evidence of facts that might have affected the outcome of the RPD hearing if the evidence has been presented to the RPD” (Raza at para 13).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds PRRA is not an appeal but assesses new risks; prior negative RPD decisions must be respected absent new evidence.

propositions.text: The RPD noted the Principal Applicant's testimony about fifteen elders in Benin City as agents of persecution.
propositions.quote: the Principal Applicant spoke of the fifteen elders who constituted the core members of the agents of persecution as being located in Benin City

propositions.text: The Principal Applicant testified that elders' large families and friends could spot the Applicants in Port Harcourt.
propositions.quote: He then testified that these elders have large families and that their friends and family members could spot the Applicants in Port Harcourt

propositions.text: The RPD found the size of the extended family did not explain how Applicants would be found in Port Harcourt, a large city far from Benin City.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that the size of the extended family did not adequately answer the question of how the Applicants would be found in Port Harcourt, a large city about a 4.5 hour drive from Benin City

propositions.text: The RPD held that a large, organized search would be needed to track Applicants in Port Harcourt, and Applicants' evidence did not explain how such a search was possible.
propositions.quote: The RPD held that it would take a large, organized search effort to track the Applicants down in a populous city so far removed from Benin City... Applicants’ evidence did not explain how such a search could be within the means of the extended family

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the Applicants' evidence insufficient to show how persecutors in Benin City could find them in Port Harcourt, a distant large city.

propositions.text: The RAD found the IFA determinative and addressed Applicants' submissions on Port Harcourt's viability.
propositions.quote: The RAD noted that the IFA was determinative. It addressed the Applicants’ submissions with respect to the viability of Port Harcourt

propositions.text: The RAD found it speculative that agents of persecution could find Applicants in Port Harcourt.
propositions.quote: It also found that it was speculative that the agents of persecution could find the Applicants in Port Harcourt

propositions.text: The Principal Applicant testified he would have to register his phone and bank withdrawals could be tracked.
propositions.quote: The Principal Applicant had testified that he would have to register his phone and that his withdrawals from banks could be tracked

propositions.text: The RAD concluded Applicants did not provide sufficient evidence that agents of persecution could trace them through transactions.
propositions.quote: The RAD concluded that the Applicants had not provided sufficient evidence to find that the agents of persecution could trace them through those transactions

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found the IFA determinative, rejected Applicants' arguments on Port Harcourt, and found insufficient evidence of tracing through transactions.

propositions.text: Applicants do not point to evidence submitted to PRRA Officer that overcomes RPD and RAD findings of viable IFA in Port Harcourt.
propositions.quote: the Applicants do not point to any evidence that they submitted to the PRRA Officer that would overcome the prior findings of the RPD and RAD that there is a viable IFA in Port Harcourt

propositions.text: PRRA Officer acknowledged Principal Applicant's affidavit stating persecutors are well connected and could easily locate Applicants.
propositions.quote: the PRRA Officer acknowledged, in the Principal Applicant’s affidavit he stated that the persecutors are very well connected across Nigeria with their and they would be able to easily locate the Applicants

propositions.text: This differs from Applicants' submissions to RPD and RAD but no explanation why argument was not previously made.
propositions.quote: This appears to differ from Applicants’ submissions to the RPD and RAD, but there is no explanation as to why this argument had not been previously made

propositions.text: Submissions to PRRA Officer focus on persecutors' ongoing interest, gender-based violence, worsening conditions, but no new risk showing IFA no longer viable.
propositions.quote: the submissions made to the PRRA Officer in support of the PRRA center the persecutors ongoing interest in the Applicants, gender-based violence and worsening country conditions without demonstrating any new risk in light of which the IFA previously identified in Port Harcourt is no longer viable

propositions.text: Applicants do not point to evidence or country conditions before PRRA Officer supporting claim persecutors are well connected with police and politicians or that they would assist in pursuing Applicants.
propositions.quote: Nor do the Applicants point to any evidence or country conditions documentation that was before the PRRA Officer to support their claim that the agents of persecution were well connected with police and politicians, or that those entities would and could assist them in pursuing their alleged ongoing interest in the Applicants

paragraphs.summary: Applicants do not provide evidence to overcome prior findings of viable IFA; PRRA submissions differ but lack explanation or new risk evidence.

propositions.text: Even if Applicants showed persecutors' ongoing interest, it would not help unless they disproved viable IFA, which they failed to do.
propositions.quote: regardless of whether the Applicants provided evidence of their persecutors ongoing interest in them, doing so could not assist them unless they also established that they did not have a viable IFA. This they failed to do

propositions.text: PRRA Officer was not required to weigh evidence of ongoing risk if viable IFA existed.
propositions.quote: the PRRA Officer was not required to weigh the evidence pertaining to the claimed ongoing risk to, and interest in, the Applicants by their persecutors

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes Applicants failed to disprove viable IFA, so PRRA Officer need not consider ongoing risk evidence.

propositions.text: PRRA Officer's reasons were succinct but reasonable when read with RPD and RAD decisions.
propositions.quote: While the PRRA Officer’s reasons were succinct, read in whole together with the record – in particular, the RPD and RAD decisions – they were reasonable

propositions.text: Judicial review application is dismissed; no costs order; no question of general importance arises.
propositions.quote: The application for judicial review is dismissed; There shall be no order as to costs; and No question of general importance for certification was proposed or arises

paragraphs.summary: Court finds PRRA Officer's reasons reasonable and dismisses judicial review application without costs or certification.
